judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade R (rank 0) Skills under Emergent Writing / Emergent Handwriting, so direction must be set by Term within the grade. The second SFI sits in Term 3 ('Holds crayons using an acceptable pencil grip and writes using a good writing position', LCs: pencil grip, writing position/posture), while the first sits in Term 4 ('Forms letters using finger paint, paint brushes, wax crayons', LC tags: crayons, finger paint, handwriting, letters). This is not mere repeated wording: Term 3 establishes tool-holding grip and writing posture, and Term 4 extends that control to actually forming letter shapes with a range of media. Secure grip and position proficiency supports success at letter formation, so the permitted earlier-Term-to-later-Term direction (second_to_first) applies. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each) and both endpoints and all ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, but the retained statement text, identity scopes and Term ancestors are consistent and sufficient for this judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills are printed bullets in the same Grade 3 (rank 3), Term 1, WRITING / 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' table (page 113), so direction cannot come from grade or term order and must rest on substantive content. 'Talks to a partner to begin planning writing' (LC tags: oral, partner talk, planning, writing) is an explicit pre-writing planning step, while 'Writes and illustrates sentences (six to eight sentences) on a topic to contribute to a book for the class library' (LCs: writes sentences on a topic; illustrates them) is the extended composition product on a topic. Oral planning with a partner is the preparatory stage of the writing process that supports producing a coherent six-to-eight-sentence topic text for a class book, so proficiency in the first supports success in the second; the reverse dependency is not supported. Judgment rests on the bounded excerpts; source evidence for both endpoints is truncated and upstream merge/audit context was inspected without changing the reading.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills are Grade R (rank 0, resolved), Term 1, Emergent Reading, under the same single parent sub-strand 'Begins to make meaning of written text', and both come from the same printed table row (row=4) on page 37. 'Understands that written words refer to spoken words' (print awareness; spoken/written words) and "'Reads' high frequency words: own name, common brand names such as SPAR, Coke, and television programme titles etc." (environmental print; high frequency words; own name) are complementary emergent print-awareness behaviours: one names the insight that print represents speech, the other names early whole-word/environmental-print recognition. That is meaningful, pair-specific instructional coherence rather than generic repetition or mere word overlap ('words' is the only shared text token). It is not, however, a justified developmental dependency: the two are concurrently listed Term 1 expectations within a single row of the same sub-strand, and the target shows no expanded scope, complexity, text length, or independence relative to the source, so the same-rank, same-Term substantive-extension bar for buildsTowards is not met in either direction. Judgment is symmetric relatesTo with canonical endpoint order preserved and null direction. Limitations: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and the Grade/Term ancestors carry merge context, though the full statement texts are present and unambiguous.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade 3 Writing under the 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' sub-strand (first: Term 4, 'Uses a dictionary to find new vocabulary and check spelling'; second: Term 2, 'Reads and edits own writing by correcting spelling, punctuation, etc.'). They cohere substantively around spelling accuracy in the learner's own written work: self-reading and correcting spelling/punctuation during editing, and using a dictionary as the reference tool for checking spelling. This is complementary skill/application coherence, not a developmental dependency: the Term 4 statement introduces a separate reference-tool capability (dictionary look-up) plus a vocabulary-building purpose, and does not expand, deepen, or increase the complexity of the Term 2 editing capability, nor does editing proficiency materially raise the likelihood of success at dictionary use. The other nomination signals (shared Grade 3 ancestor, zero rank gap, a single shared 'spelling' LC/text token, spelling-driven trigram overlap) are hierarchy/wording evidence only and cannot establish progression. Accordingly relatesTo (symmetric, null direction) with canonical endpoint order preserved. Both endpoints have truncated source evidence and upstream audit/merge context, which limits certainty.

judgment.rationale: First SFI (resolved coordinate Grade 1, rank 1): Term 2 / WRITING / Shared, Group and Independent Writing — 'Writes one sentence of own news or shared writing'. Second SFI (resolved coordinate Grade 1, rank 1): Term 4 / LISTENING AND SPEAKING (ORAL) / Daily-Weekly activities — 'Uses terms such as sentence, capital letter, full stop'. The two share a substantive, pair-specific focus on the sentence as a unit: the Term 4 oral item names precisely the conventions (sentence boundary, capital letter, full stop) that govern the written sentence produced in the Term 2 writing bullet, so the metalinguistic vocabulary and the composing task reinforce one another as complementary oral and written treatments of the same object. This is more than shared wording or shared hierarchy. However, the evidence does not support a developmental dependency: the oral terminology item is not an expanded, longer, more independent, or otherwise deepened version of composing one sentence of own news, and the linking signals (one shared token 'sentence', SFI-text Jaccard 0.059, LC-tag Jaccard 0.143, token-derived trigrams, shared Grade ancestor, weak rank proximity with gap 0) do not show that proficiency in one supports success in the other. Accordingly the judgment is symmetric relatesTo with null direction, preserving canonical endpoint order. Material limitations: both endpoints are truncated with 24 omitted source-evidence items each, which could not be inspected and whose absence from the excerpt is not proof of absence in the source; all endpoint and ancestor nodes (including merged Grade 1 and Term banner nodes and the adjudicated Writing / Listening-and-Speaking sub-strands) carry upstream audit/merge/code context that is retained unresolved below.

This is not mere repeated wording: the Term 1 statement introduces the single, highly patterned case of a written-but-unpronounced letter within the split-digraph vowel pattern, while the Term 3 statement generalises the same principle to an unpredictable set of silent consonants in word-initial and word-final positions, a substantive broadening of word-recognition demand. Shared LC tags (phonics, word recognition, silent) corroborate the conceptual continuity, so Term 1 proficiency plausibly supports success in the Term 3 skill. judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade 3 (rank 3) Skills under LISTENING AND SPEAKING (ORAL): the first is Term 1, sub-strand 'Twice weekly focussed listening and speaking activities' — 'Listens to a complex sequence of instructions (at least 4) and responds appropriately' (LCs: listens to a complex sequence of instructions (at least 4); responds appropriately to a complex sequence of instructions); the second is Term 2, sub-strand 'Daily / Weekly activities in all areas of Language and other subjects' — 'Listens and responds to radio or intercom announcements and instructions' (LCs: listens to radio or intercom announcements and instructions; responds to radio or intercom announcements and instructions). The pair shares a specific, instructionally useful core: aural comprehension of spoken instructions followed by an appropriate action/response, applied in two complementary classroom contexts (focussed oral instruction-following vs. responding to broadcast announcements). This is more than generic repetition or shared Grade/Skill Area hierarchy, so no_relation is not warranted. However, the evidence does not show substantive extension: the Term 2 statement does not specify more steps, longer or more complex input, or greater independence, and the shift from face-to-face instruction sequences to radio/intercom announcements is a change of medium and routine rather than an evidenced increase in demand (a short announcement may be less demanding than a four-step sequence). Without evidenced deepening or broadening of capability, proficiency in the Term 1 skill cannot be said to support likelihood of success in the Term 2 skill, so buildsTowards is not justified and symmetric relatesTo is the correct judgment. judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit in Grade 1 (rank 1), Term 1, but in different Skill Areas: 'Reads labels and captions in the classroom' under Reading and Phonics / Emergent reading skills, and 'Copies and writes own name, short words and sentences from labels, posters, chalkboard etc.' under Writing / Handwriting. They share the classroom print environment (labels, posters) as the common material, making them genuinely complementary reading-and-writing uses of environmental print rather than a dependency: the writing statement is about fine-motor copying and letter formation, which is not conditioned on independent reading of captions, and the reading statement does not require handwriting proficiency. Same grade and same term provide no admissible developmental ordering, and the lexical overlap is limited to 'labels' and 'and', so the evidence supports substantive conceptual coherence only. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each) and both carry upstream merge/audit context, so no stronger developmental claim is warranted.
